items.topic: Natural gas marketers vs. physical companies
items.definition: Marketers are the speculative traders of the natural gas world — often Wall Street firms or spinoffs from energy companies — who buy and sell gas to profit from price moves, as distinct from physical companies that produce, move, or store the commodity itself.
items.core_idea: Physical natural gas businesses generally prefer to earn steady profits in a specialized, hard-to-enter niche and leave speculative trading to dedicated marketers, because trading's volatility conflicts with the steady-earnings expectations of a service company's shareholders.
key_points: Many gas-services companies have shrunk or closed trading desks because a few bad trades can threaten an otherwise stable business.
Physical companies still keep some trading capability, mainly to hedge price risk on the raw materials they already hold.
Physical companies occasionally trade speculatively, since their domain expertise can let them spot opportunities before others.
Marketers require deep operational/legal infrastructure: contracts, credit monitoring, and relationships across many counterparties, plus arranging storage and transportation logistics.
Because of their broad contact networks, marketers tend to trade across many commodities (electricity, coal, oil, emissions credits), not just natural gas.
trading_implications: A marketer's competitive edge comes from breadth of counterparty relationships and logistics/legal capability, not just price views.
A physical producer's trading activity is usually risk-reducing (hedging) rather than a profit center.
common_misunderstandings: That physical energy companies don't trade at all — they do, but mostly to hedge, not to speculate.

items.topic: Segments of the physical natural gas business
items.definition: The natural gas industry is organized into distinct functional segments, each handling a different stage of moving gas from underground reservoir to end consumer.
items.core_idea: Natural gas moves through seven broad functions: exploration, drilling, processing, interstate pipeline transport, LNG transport, storage, and distribution.
key_points: Exploration: searching for new natural gas sources.
Drilling: extracting gas from underground reservoirs and moving it to processing plants.
Processing: converting raw gas into a standardized commodity (nearly pure methane, called dry natural gas).
Interstate pipeline transportation: maintaining pipelines linking producing areas or LNG terminals to consuming regions.
LNG transportation: shipping gas across oceans by tanker after cooling it to about -260°F to liquefy it.
Storage: maintaining large underground facilities to hold natural gas.
Distribution: delivering gas from a transporter or storage facility to end consumers.
relationships: Gas value chain segments feed into each other sequentially, from wellhead to consumer
trading_implications: Each segment represents a distinct point where price risk, basis risk, or capacity constraints can arise (e.g., pipeline vs. storage vs. LNG bottlenecks).

items.topic: Formation and trapping of natural gas
items.definition: Natural gas forms from decaying organic material and becomes economically recoverable only when an impermeable rock layer prevents the resulting methane from escaping to the surface.
items.core_idea: Methane is a common byproduct of decomposing organic matter; it normally disperses into the atmosphere, but when trapped beneath impermeable rock it accumulates underground, dispersed through small connected pores rather than pooling in an open cavern.
key_points: Natural gas is often found dissolved in oil fields, coal beds, and underground rock formations.
Underground deposits can be millions of years old, but methane can also form quickly from modern decomposing waste (e.g., landfills).
Trapped gas typically resides dispersed in small holes of a porous rock layer, not in a large open cavity.
Exploration targets a permeable rock layer sitting beneath an impermeable cap layer, since gas must be able to flow toward a well to be extracted.
common_misunderstandings: That underground gas deposits are large open caves rather than gas dispersed through porous rock.

items.topic: Reservoir pressure and well production decline
items.definition: The rate at which a natural gas well produces is driven by the pressure differential between the reservoir and the surface, which naturally declines as the reservoir is depleted.
items.core_idea: Gas flows from high to low pressure, so a well produces fastest when the reservoir is freshest (highest pressure) and slows over time as pressure drops, eventually reaching a point where continued extraction is no longer economical and the well is closed.
key_points: A vacuum applied at the reservoir mouth combines with gas's natural buoyancy to pull it upward.
Production rate is fastest immediately after a well is opened and decreases as reservoir pressure falls.
Water injection can be used to artificially raise the pressure of remaining gas, since methane doesn't dissolve in water — this can extend a well's productive life.
The physical properties of the reservoir rock directly affect how quickly gas can be recovered.
trading_implications: Declining well productivity over time is a structural driver of ongoing drilling activity needed to sustain supply.

items.definition: Porosity is the proportion of a rock's total volume that consists of empty space (holes), usually expressed as a percentage.
items.core_idea: Porosity measures how much void space a rock contains, which affects how much gas it can potentially hold, but says nothing on its own about whether that gas can be extracted.
key_points: Nearly all rock has some porosity, but the amount, size, and type of pores vary widely by rock type.
Porosity alone does not determine whether gas can flow out of the rock — that depends on permeability.
common_misunderstandings: That high porosity by itself implies a rock is a good gas producer — it must also be permeable.

_validation.judge_reason: Source confirms porosity refers to pore holes storing gas and permeability (connectedness) as separate factor for extraction, matching the item's definition and key points.

items.definition: Permeability describes how interconnected a rock's pores are, i.e., how easily fluid can move through the rock structure.
items.core_idea: A rock can be porous without being permeable, since porosity measures the amount of void space while permeability measures whether those voids connect enough to let gas or liquid flow through.
key_points: Permeability is typically assessed by how readily a liquid passes through the porous material.
Example given by the author: a foam coffee cup is highly porous (trapped air insulates well) but has low permeability (liquid doesn't leak through).
common_misunderstandings: Confusing porosity (amount of holes) with permeability (connectivity between holes) — they are independent properties.

items.definition: Hydraulic fracturing is a technique for extracting gas from rock that is porous but not naturally permeable, by artificially creating fractures that connect the pores.
items.core_idea: By injecting water or similar fluid and using controlled explosions to generate compression waves, engineers create microfractures throughout a rock formation, making an otherwise impermeable but porous rock permeable enough for conventional drilling to extract the gas.
key_points: Targets rock that has gas trapped in pores but lacks the interconnection needed for the gas to flow to a well.
The fracturing process itself doesn't extract the gas — it enables extraction via conventional drilling afterward.
trading_implications: Fracking technology expanded economically recoverable gas supply by unlocking previously inaccessible porous-but-impermeable formations.

items.topic: Natural gas processing and quality standards
items.definition: Raw natural gas from the wellhead is not pure methane and must be processed to remove impurities and meet a standardized energy-content specification before it can enter pipelines or reach consumers.
items.core_idea: Processing strips out particulates, liquid water, and trace pollutants (e.g., hydrogen sulfide, mercury), and brings the gas to a consistent heating value so it is safe for pipelines/equipment and tradeable as a standardized commodity.
key_points: Impurities like particulate matter and liquid water must be removed to prevent pipeline and equipment damage.
Trace pollutants such as hydrogen sulfide and mercury must be removed.
In North America, consumer-grade natural gas must have a heat content of about 1,035 Btu per cubic foot, plus or minus 5 percent, measured at standard temperature and pressure.

trading_implications: The Btu specification is the basis for gas being treated as a fungible, standardized commodity across the pipeline grid.

items.definition: Processing plants separate a raw hydrocarbon mixture into its individual components by exploiting the fact that different hydrocarbons liquefy (reach their dew point) at different temperatures.
items.core_idea: Because larger hydrocarbon molecules like propane and butane turn liquid at warmer temperatures than smaller ones like methane, progressively cooling the raw gas stream causes the larger molecules to condense out first, allowing them to be separated from the gas before it enters the pipeline.
key_points: Larger hydrocarbons (e.g., propane, butane) must be removed so they don't condense into liquid within a pipeline.
Separation is achieved by progressively cooling the combined gas stream so each component liquefies at its own characteristic temperature.
trading_implications: This separation process is what produces natural gas liquids (NGLs) like propane and butane as distinct tradeable commodities from raw gas.
